title: Physical Chemistry
lines: Physical chemistry questions in USAT mix concepts and short calculations: shapes of molecules and hybridisation, enthalpy changes and Hess's law, equilibrium constants and Le Chatelier's principle, pH, rate laws and half-lives, cell potentials and electrolysis, and the properties of solutions. Learn the rules in each area and the few formulas that go with them.
## Chemical bonding

- Ionic bonds form by electron transfer, usually when the electronegativity difference is about 1.7 or more. Covalent bonds share electron pairs. In a coordinate bond both shared electrons come from one atom (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺).
- Electronegativity: F (4.0) > O > N ≈ Cl > C > H.
- VSEPR: electron pairs repel and spread out; lone pairs repel more than bond pairs, squeezing the bond angles.
| Molecule | Pairs (bond, lone) | Shape, angle
| BeCl₂, CO₂ | 2, 0 | linear, 180°
| BF₃ | 3, 0 | trigonal planar, 120°
| CH₄ | 4, 0 | tetrahedral, 109.5°
| NH₃ | 3, 1 | pyramidal, about 107°
- Hybridisation: sp (linear), sp² (trigonal planar), sp³ (tetrahedral). A single bond is one σ bond; a double bond is σ + π; a triple bond is σ + 2π.
- A molecule with polar bonds can have zero dipole moment if it is symmetrical (CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄).
## Thermochemistry
- Exothermic: ΔH negative. Endothermic: ΔH positive. Standard conditions: 298 K and 1 atm.

- The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero. Enthalpy of combustion is always negative. Neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base gives about −57 kJ per mole of water.
- Hess's law: the total enthalpy change is the same whatever route is taken. ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔH(f, products) − ΣΔH(f, reactants).
> Example 1. C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −394 kJ/mol. CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283 kJ/mol. Find ΔH for C + ½O₂ → CO.
> Take the first equation and subtract the second: ΔH = −394 − (−283) = −111 kJ/mol.
## Chemical equilibrium
- At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal).
- For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ. Pure solids and liquids are left out. Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the change in moles of gas.
- K changes only with temperature. Reversing the equation gives 1/K.

- Le Chatelier: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change. Adding a reactant shifts it forward; raising pressure favours fewer gas moles; heating favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst does not shift the position; it only brings equilibrium sooner.
## Acids, bases and pH
- Arrhenius acids give H⁺ in water. Brønsted-Lowry acids donate protons; bases accept them. Lewis acids accept an electron pair (BF₃, AlCl₃); Lewis bases donate one (NH₃).
- pH = −log[H⁺]. At 25 °C, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ and pH + pOH = 14.
- A buffer (a weak acid with its salt, or a weak base with its salt) resists changes in pH. pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).
- Salts of a strong acid and a weak base (NH₄Cl) are acidic; salts of a weak acid and a strong base (CH₃COONa) are basic.
- Solubility product: a precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds Ksp. For AgCl, Ksp = s².
> Example 2. Find the pH of 0.005 M H₂SO₄, assuming complete ionisation.
> Each H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺, so [H⁺] = 0.010 M = 10⁻² M and pH = 2.
## Chemical kinetics
- Rate = change in concentration per unit time. Rate law: rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ; the overall order is x + y and comes from experiment, not from the balanced equation.
- Units of k: zero order mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, first order s⁻¹, second order dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
- First-order half-life t½ = 0.693/k does not depend on the starting concentration. Radioactive decay is first order.
- Rate rises with concentration, temperature, surface area and a catalyst. A catalyst lowers the activation energy by giving a new path; it does not change ΔH or K.
> Example 3. A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 min⁻¹. Find its half-life and the fraction left after 30 minutes.
> t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.0693 = 10 min. 30 minutes is 3 half-lives, so (½)³ = ⅛ remains.
## Electrochemistry
- Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation number rises); reduction is gain of electrons. The oxidising agent is itself reduced.
- Oxidation number rules: elements 0; O usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H usually +1 (−1 in metal hydrides); the sum equals the charge.

- In a galvanic cell chemical energy becomes electrical energy; the anode (oxidation) is negative. E°(cell) = E°(cathode) − E°(anode); a positive value means the reaction is feasible. Daniell cell: E° = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
- In electrolysis the cathode is negative and reduction happens there. Faraday's laws: 1 F = 96,500 C is the charge on one mole of electrons; mass deposited = (M × Q) ÷ (n × F).
> Example 4. A charge of 0.5 F is passed through CuSO₄ solution. What mass of copper is deposited (Cu = 63.5)?
> Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.5 F deposits 0.25 mol = 0.25 × 63.5 ≈ 15.9 g.
## Solutions
- Molarity = moles of solute per dm³ of solution; molality = moles of solute per kg of solvent; mole fraction = moles of one component ÷ total moles.
- Raoult's law: the vapour pressure of a solvent is proportional to its mole fraction. A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure.

- Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their nature: lowering of vapour pressure, rise in boiling point (ΔT = Kb m), fall in freezing point (ΔT = Kf m) and osmotic pressure. NaCl counts as two particles per formula.
! A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally; it never changes the equilibrium yield.
! Order cannot be read from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
! The anode is negative in a galvanic cell but positive in an electrolytic cell; oxidation happens at the anode in both.
## Quick check
- Shape and bond angle of BF₃? (trigonal planar, 120°)
- pH of 0.001 M NaOH? (11)
- Effect of a catalyst on ΔH? (none)
- Charge on one mole of electrons? (96,500 C)
- Which has the larger freezing-point depression, 0.1 molal glucose or 0.1 molal NaCl? (NaCl)
